"'''Say You, Say Me'''" is a song written and recorded by American singer and songwriter [[Lionel Richie]] for the film ''[[White Nights (1985 film)|White Nights]]''.<ref name="British Hit Singles & Albums">{{cite book | first= David | last= Roberts | year= 2006 | title= British Hit Singles & Albums | edition= 19th | publisher= Guinness World Records Limited | location= London | isbn= 1-904994-10-5 | page= 136}}</ref> The single hit number one on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]]<ref name=BB_Hot100/> and on the [[Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs|Hot Black Singles]] chart<ref name="HotRB"/> in December 1985. It also became Richie's ninth number-one on the ''Billboard'' [[Adult Contemporary (chart)|Adult Contemporary]] chart.<ref>{{cite book |title= Top Adult Contemporary: 1961-2001|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2002 |publisher=Record Research |page=204}}</ref><ref name="BillboardAdultContemporary"/> The track is not available on the film's [[White Nights (soundtrack)|soundtrack album]], as [[Motown]] did not want Richie's first single following the massive success of his 1983 album ''[[Can't Slow Down (Lionel Richie album)|Can't Slow Down]]'' to appear on another label. It was included by Motown on Richie's 1986 release ''[[Dancing on the Ceiling]]''.

"Say You, Say Me" is a song written and recorded by American singer and songwriter Lionel Richie for the film White Nights. The single hit number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and on the Hot Black Singles chart in December 1985. It also became Richie's ninth number-one on the Billboard Adult Contemporary chart. The track is not available on the film's soundtrack album, as Motown did not want Richie's first single following the massive success of his 1983 album Can't Slow Down to appear on another label. It was included by Motown on Richie's 1986 release Dancing on the Ceiling.

sections.heading: Development and production
sections.wikitext: For the 1985 film ''[[White Nights (1985 film)|White Nights]]'', a ballet drama starring [[Mikhail Baryshnikov]] and [[Gregory Hines]], director [[Taylor Hackford]] asked Richie to write a title theme. Unable to compose a song with "White Nights" in the title, Richie submitted a demo of the ballad "Say You, Say Me". Eventually, Hackford approved the song and included the completed version in ''White Nights''. Produced by Richie and [[James Anthony Carmichael]], the song was primarily recorded in Richie's living room.<ref name="Hogan">{{cite web|last=Hogan|first=Ed|title=Say You, Say Me|url=https://www.allmusic.com/song/say-you-say-me-mt0030399082|publisher=Allmusic|accessdate=February 16, 2021}}</ref><ref name="Holden">{{cite web|last=Holden|first=Stephen|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/08/20/arts/the-pop-life-lionel-richie-s-latest-songs-have-a-new-slant.html|title=Lionel Richie's latest songs have a new slant|work=The New York Times|date=August 20, 1986|accessdate=February 16, 2021}}</ref> "Say You, Say Me" made its official radio debut in [[Chicago, Illinois]], on then-Top 40 radio station [[WLS-FM]] on October 15, in connection of the ''White Nights'' world premiere at the 1985 [[Chicago International Film Festival]]. In the movie itself, "Say You, Say Me" was introduced over the closing credits.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-04-10-ca-1407-story.html|title=Commentary: The trouble with Oscar|work=Los Angeles Times|last=Mathews|first=Jack|date=April 10, 1988|accessdate=February 17, 2021}}</reF>

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
For ''[[The New York Times]]'' in 1986, [[Stephen Holden]] called the song "a powerful mid-80's echo of [[the Beatles]]' late-60's chant-like ballads."<ref name="Holden"/> In a mixed review of ''Dancing on the Ceiling'', Mike Joyce of ''[[The Washington Post]]'' called the song "silly and horrendously overexposed."<ref name="WaPo">{{cite news|last=Joyce|first=Mike|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/style/1986/08/17/recordings/450a0963-1fb2-44ba-bcdb-fe7196ac2262/|title=Recordings|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=August 17, 1986|accessdate=February 17, 2021}}</ref>

In a 2007 retrospective of the January 11, 1986 ''Billboard'' Hot 100 chart, Whitney Pastorek of ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' graded "Say You, Say Me" with an A-minus, calling it "an enduring love song" and commenting "the cranked-up electric bridge alone should be enough to make it a classic."<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://ew.com/article/2007/01/09/this-week-86-rating-top-10-hits/|last=Pastorek|first=Whitney|title=This week in '86: Rating the top 10 hits|magazine=Entertainment Weekly|date=January 9, 2007|accessdate=February 17, 2021|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070114010352/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20007619,00.html|archivedate=January 14, 2007|url-status=live}}</reF>

In 2008, the song was ranked at number 74 of the top songs of all time on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] chart, commemorating the first 50 years of the chart.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Billboard Hot 100 Chart 50th Anniversary - All-Time Top Songs|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081101133040/http://www.billboard.com/bbcom/specials/hot100/charts/top100-titles-80.shtml|archive-date=November 1, 2008|url-status=dead|url=http://www.billboard.com/articles/list/2155531/the-hot-100-all-time-top-songs?list_page=1|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|access-date=August 26, 2015|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
sections.text:
For The New York Times in 1986, Stephen Holden called the song "a powerful mid-80's echo of the Beatles' late-60's chant-like ballads." In a mixed review of Dancing on the Ceiling, Mike Joyce of The Washington Post called the song "silly and horrendously overexposed."

In a 2007 retrospective of the January 11, 1986 Billboard Hot 100 chart, Whitney Pastorek of Entertainment Weekly graded "Say You, Say Me" with an A-minus, calling it "an enduring love song" and commenting "the cranked-up electric bridge alone should be enough to make it a classic."

sections.heading: Commercial performance
sections.wikitext:
In the US, the "Say You, Say Me" single sold a million copies and was no. 1 for two weeks on the ''Billboard'' "Hot Black" chart and for four weeks on the Hot 100.<ref name="Hogan"/>

The single was hugely successful in South Africa, attaining the No. 1 spot on the weekly charts for a total of 30 weeks. It was the No. 1 single of 1986 on the year-end Springbok chart.

In 2012, Lionel Richie re-recorded the song with Danish [[pop music|pop]] singer-songwriter [[Rasmus Seebach]].<ref>{{cite web|first=Sine|last=Lundbech|url=http://gaffa.dk/nyhed/57899|title=Lionel Richie og Seebach-duet udkommer verden over|date=February 23, 2012|work=[[Gaffa (magazine)|Gaffa]]|access-date=March 2, 2012|language=da|archive-date=October 9, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191009114458/https://gaffa.dk/nyhed/57899|url-status=dead}}</ref> The duet is featured on Richie's album ''[[Tuskegee (album)|Tuskegee]]'', for which Richie has picked a host of best-selling singers from around the world in collaborations. The album version features American country singer [[Jason Aldean]].<ref>[http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/earshot/lionel-richie-duet-rasmus-seebach-say-you-say-me-293960 ''Hollywood Reporter'': Lionel Richie Teams With Danish Sensation Rasmus Seebach to Breathe New Life Into a Classic (Video)]</ref>

In 2012, Lionel Richie re-recorded the song with Danish pop singer-songwriter Rasmus Seebach. The duet is featured on Richie's album Tuskegee, for which Richie has picked a host of best-selling singers from around the world in collaborations. The album version features American country singer Jason Aldean.
